messages.subject: Estimating variance-covariance LKJ
parts:
Dear all,

I am trying to fit a CMR-model in nimble where I estimate temporal sex-specific survival with a variance - covariance matrix for the sexes using the LKJ-distribution.
The model runs fine, but it doesn't sample for the first column of the correlation matrix (Ustar). I have tried different initial-values but it doesnt seem to make a difference.
I have also encountered the same problem with other models where the variance - covariance matrix is much bigger, where the first value, Ustar[1,1] doesnt sample.

Would appreciate any help with this! Model code and summary of variance-covariance parameters are below.

Cheers
Christoffer

 MCMCsummary(samples, params = c("U", "Ustar", "sigma"))
                 mean        sd        2.5%       50%     97.5% Rhat n.eff
U[1, 1]     1.3330221 0.6748026  0.38272517 1.1844371 3.2310965 1.25    73
U[2, 1]     0.0000000 0.0000000  0.00000000 0.0000000 0.0000000  NaN     0
U[1, 2]     0.1187551 0.4920896 -0.82181479 0.0559964 1.3018353 1.32   138
U[2, 2]     0.7870212 0.7113290  0.07996239 0.6304792 2.8114862 2.16    26
Ustar[1, 1] 0.5000000 0.0000000  0.50000000 0.5000000 0.5000000  NaN     0
Ustar[2, 1] 0.0000000 0.0000000  0.00000000 0.0000000 0.0000000  NaN     0
Ustar[1, 2] 0.1017624 0.4409135 -0.82087382 0.1308377 0.8417357 1.06    87
Ustar[2, 2] 0.8787592 0.1521770  0.43725731 0.9434168 0.9997267 1.07    90
sigma[1]    2.6660441 1.3496051  0.76545033 2.3688742 6.4621929 1.25    73
sigma[2]    0.8831785 0.7755968  0.12913382 0.7075327 3.0124881 2.22    27
>


nimbleCode({
 
  for (i in 1:N) {
    for (t in 1:(T - 1)) {
     
      logit(phi[i, t]) <- eta.phi[t, sex[i]]
      gamma[1, 1, t, i] <- phi[i, t] # Pr(alive t -> alive t+1)
      gamma[1, 2, t, i] <- 1 - phi[i, t] # Pr(alive t -> dead t+1)
      gamma[2, 1, t, i] <- 0 # Pr(dead t -> alive t+1)
      gamma[2, 2, t, i] <- 1 # Pr(dead t -> dead t+1)
     
      logit(p[i, t]) <- alpha[1] + alpha[2]*sex[i] + eps_p[t]
      omega[1, 1, t, i] <- 1 - p[i, t] # Pr(alive t -> non-detected t)
      omega[1, 2, t, i] <- p[i, t] # Pr(alive t -> detected t)
      omega[2, 1, t, i] <- 1 # Pr(dead t -> non-detected t)
      omega[2, 2, t, i] <- 0 # Pr(dead t -> detected t)
    }
  }
 
  delta[1] <- 1 # Pr(alive t = 1) = 1
  delta[2] <- 0 # Pr(dead t = 1) = 0
 
  for (u in 1:2){
    mean.phi[u] ~ dbeta(1,1)
    mu.phi[u] <- log(mean.phi[u] / (1-mean.phi[u]))
    sigma[u] ~ dunif(0,10)
  }
 
 
  Ustar[1:2,1:2] ~ dlkj_corr_cholesky(1.3, p = 2) # upper triangular Cholesky factor - correlation matrix
  U[1:2,1:2] <- uppertri_mult_diag(Ustar[1:2, 1:2], sigma[1:2]) # U is the covariance matrix
  for(t in 1:(T-1))
    eta.phi[t, 1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu.phi[1:2], cholesky = U[1:2, 1:2], prec_param = 0)
 
 
  for (u in 1:2) {
    alpha[u] ~ dnorm(mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
  }
 
  for (t in 1:(T-1)){
    eps_p[t] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sdeps_p)
  }
 
  sdeps_p ~ dunif(0,10)
 
  for (t in 1:(T-1)){
    p_female[t] <- 1/(1+exp(-(alpha[1]+eps_p[t])))
    p_male[t] <- 1/(1+exp(-(alpha[1]+alpha[2]+eps_p[t])))
  }
 
  # likelihood
  for (i in 1:N) {
    z[i, first[i]] ~ dcat(delta[1:2])
    for (j in (first[i] + 1):(T-1)) {
      z[i, j] ~ dcat(gamma[z[i, j - 1], 1:2, j - 1, i])
      y[i, j] ~ dcat(omega[z[i, j], 1:2, j - 1, i])
    }
  }
})

messages.subject: Re: Estimating variance-covariance LKJ
parts:
Hi Christoffer,

A few comments about the LKJ distribution:

- Ustar is the **Cholesky** decomposition of the correlation matrix. That means that since the correlations are 1, there is actually only one free variable in the 2x2 matrix, which determines the correlation. You see that both Ustar[1,2] and Ustar[2,2] are changing, but the values are constrained such that you should be able to verify that the square of Ustar[1,2] plus the square of Ustar[2,2] equals 1 for every MCMC iteration. 
- If you did want to reconstruct the correlation matrix yourself by matrix multiplication, note that Ustar[1,1] should be equal to 1 and Ustar[2,1] should be equal to 0 before you do the multiplication. I see that Ustar[1,1] equals 0.5 in your results. Did you initialize Ustar[1,1] to 0.5?  I am thinking that we might need to say a bit more in our documentation about this!
- In terms of the MCMC results, it's fine that Ustar[1,1] equals 0.5 because dlkj_corr_cholesky actually ignores Ustar[1,1] (and Ustar[2,1]).

-chris

parts:
Yes, I have a note to myself to give more details in the manual. I'm also seeing that the grammar of one of the sentences in the manual could be quite confusing. It should say "convert it to the upper triangular Cholesky factor (U) of a covariance matrix".

As far as your questions, to calculate the correlation matrix, you need to calculate it on a per-iteration basis, t(Ustar)%*%Ustar, where "Ustar" is the Ustar from a single iteration and Ustar[1,1]=1 and Ustar[2,1]=0. (It looks like you are calculating t(Ustar)%*%Ustar with the posterior means, which is not correct.) That will give you the posterior samples of the correlation matrix. If you want the posterior samples of the correlation, then just take the [1,2] (or [2,1]) elements of these matrices. However, in this simple 2x2 case one can also get the correlation parameter simply as the Ustar[1,2] element from each iteration, which has a posterior mean of 0.0088 in this case as you say.

I don't know why it is low when you expect it to be higher.  One thing you could try is simulating data from a model with a high correlation and see if the MCMC applied to simulated data recovers the true parameters, in particular the correlation, well.

nimbleCode({
 
  for (i in 1:N) {
    for (t in 1:(T - 1)) {
     
      logit(phi[i, t]) <- eta.phi[t, sex[i]]
      gamma[1, 1, t, i] <- phi[i, t] # Pr(alive t -> alive t+1)
      gamma[1, 2, t, i] <- 1 - phi[i, t] # Pr(alive t -> dead t+1)
      gamma[2, 1, t, i] <- 0 # Pr(dead t -> alive t+1)
      gamma[2, 2, t, i] <- 1 # Pr(dead t -> dead t+1)
     
      logit(p[i, t]) <- alpha[1] + alpha[2]*sex[i] + eps_p[t]
      omega[1, 1, t, i] <- 1 - p[i, t] # Pr(alive t -> non-detected t)
      omega[1, 2, t, i] <- p[i, t] # Pr(alive t -> detected t)
      omega[2, 1, t, i] <- 1 # Pr(dead t -> non-detected t)
      omega[2, 2, t, i] <- 0 # Pr(dead t -> detected t)
    }
  }
 
  delta[1] <- 1 # Pr(alive t = 1) = 1
  delta[2] <- 0 # Pr(dead t = 1) = 0
 
  for (u in 1:2){
    mean.phi[u] ~ dbeta(1,1)
    mu.phi[u] <- log(mean.phi[u] / (1-mean.phi[u]))
    sigma[u] ~ dunif(0,10)
  }
 
 
  Ustar[1:2,1:2] ~ dlkj_corr_cholesky(1.3, p = 2) # upper triangular Cholesky factor - correlation matrix
  U[1:2,1:2] <- uppertri_mult_diag(Ustar[1:2, 1:2], sigma[1:2]) # U is the covariance matrix
  for(t in 1:(T-1))
    eta.phi[t, 1:2] ~ dmnorm(mu.phi[1:2], cholesky = U[1:2, 1:2], prec_param = 0)
 
 
  for (u in 1:2) {
    alpha[u] ~ dnorm(mean = 0, sd = 1.5)
  }
 
  for (t in 1:(T-1)){
    eps_p[t] ~ dnorm(0, sd = sdeps_p)
  }
 
  sdeps_p ~ dunif(0,10)
 
  for (t in 1:(T-1)){
    p_female[t] <- 1/(1+exp(-(alpha[1]+eps_p[t])))
    p_male[t] <- 1/(1+exp(-(alpha[1]+alpha[2]+eps_p[t])))
  }
 
  # likelihood
  for (i in 1:N) {
    z[i, first[i]] ~ dcat(delta[1:2])
    for (j in (first[i] + 1):(T-1)) {
      z[i, j] ~ dcat(gamma[z[i, j - 1], 1:2, j - 1, i])
      y[i, j] ~ dcat(omega[z[i, j], 1:2, j - 1, i])
    }
  }
})

On Friday 2 February 2024 at 17:43:53 UTC+1 Chris Paciorek wrote:
Yes, I have a note to myself to give more details in the manual. I'm also seeing that the grammar of one of the sentences in the manual could be quite confusing. It should say "convert it to the upper triangular Cholesky factor (U) of a covariance matrix".

As far as your questions, to calculate the correlation matrix, you need to calculate it on a per-iteration basis, t(Ustar)%*%Ustar, where "Ustar" is the Ustar from a single iteration and Ustar[1,1]=1 and Ustar[2,1]=0. (It looks like you are calculating t(Ustar)%*%Ustar with the posterior means, which is not correct.) That will give you the posterior samples of the correlation matrix. If you want the posterior samples of the correlation, then just take the [1,2] (or [2,1]) elements of these matrices. However, in this simple 2x2 case one can also get the correlation parameter simply as the Ustar[1,2] element from each iteration, which has a posterior mean of 0.0088 in this case as you say.

I don't know why it is low when you expect it to be higher.  One thing you could try is simulating data from a model with a high correlation and see if the MCMC applied to simulated data recovers the true parameters, in particular the correlation, well.

On Wednesday 31 January 2024 at 02:43:43 UTC+1 Chris Paciorek wrote:
Hi Christoffer,

A few comments about the LKJ distribution:

- Ustar is the **Cholesky** decomposition of the correlation matrix. That means that since the correlations are 1, there is actually only one free variable in the 2x2 matrix, which determines the correlation. You see that both Ustar[1,2] and Ustar[2,2] are changing, but the values are constrained such that you should be able to verify that the square of Ustar[1,2] plus the square of Ustar[2,2] equals 1 for every MCMC iteration. 
- If you did want to reconstruct the correlation matrix yourself by matrix multiplication, note that Ustar[1,1] should be equal to 1 and Ustar[2,1] should be equal to 0 before you do the multiplication. I see that Ustar[1,1] equals 0.5 in your results. Did you initialize Ustar[1,1] to 0.5?  I am thinking that we might need to say a bit more in our documentation about this!
- In terms of the MCMC results, it's fine that Ustar[1,1] equals 0.5 because dlkj_corr_cholesky actually ignores Ustar[1,1] (and Ustar[2,1]).

-chris
